note: claude-opus-5-5、入力 3254 / 出力 2876 トークン

data.question: Should we adopt the rule change block_k 3 → 2, which B and C voted against; adopt the contract change that relaxes the pickup promise from 120 s to 150 s; or keep the current rules and contract?
data.background: Option 1 passed check, constitution and the KPI conditions, and improved on_time_deliveries by +9.2 on 5/5 seeds. However, B and C voted it down, and overriding or renegotiating a company vote is a decision for the human operators, not for me. Option 3 changes the customer promise (DELIVERY_SLA). Customers do not vote, and the KPI requires a human to accept a looser promise only after seeing its measured same-seed effect on customer waits, so I cannot adopt it myself either.

options.summary: Evict a parked robot when 2 (not 3) robots are waiting behind it. On-time rises from 121.8 to 131.0 (+9.2, 5/5 seeds) and late falls from 10.4 to 1.2. Blocked s falls from 2404 to 985, and the lowest on-time rate rises from 0.84 to 0.98. Customer waits improve: p95_wait_s goes from 188 to 81.4 and max_wait_s from 385 to 245, while unfinished stays at 0.0. Road violations rise from 25.8 to 34.0. Votes were A ○, B ×, C ×.
options.stakeholders: Customers gain the most: more orders arrive on time and actual waits are much shorter, with no change to their promise. A gains (utility 38.4 → 45.4). B loses slightly (38.9 → 37.2). C loses heavily (28.8 → 19.0), presumably because its robots are evicted more often. Other road users may bear the cost of more road violations (25.8 → 34.0).

options.summary: Relax the pickup promise from 120 s to 150 s. On-time rises from 121.8 to 122.6 (+0.8, only 3/5 seeds) and late falls from 10.4 to 9.6. Blocked s (2404) and road violations (25.8) are unchanged. p95_wait_s 188, max_wait_s 385 and unfinished 0.0 are all unchanged. All three companies voted ○.
options.stakeholders: Customers do not wait any less. They receive a weaker promise, and the small on-time gain comes from redefining what counts as on time, not from faster service. All companies gain slightly (A 38.4 → 39.0, B 38.9 → 39.1, C unchanged at 28.8) and face fewer late penalties. The underlying blocking problem is not addressed.

options.summary: Stay at v1. On-time stays at 121.8, late at 10.4, blocked s at 2404, p95_wait_s at 188, max_wait_s at 385 and unfinished at 0.0.
options.stakeholders: Customers keep the current promise but keep the long waits and the roughly 10 late deliveries. Companies keep their current utilities (38.4 / 38.9 / 28.8). No one is newly harmed, and no one benefits.

recommendation.reason: Option 1 is the only option that substantially advances the main goal (+9.2 on-time, 5/5 seeds). It also improves every customer-facing watched metric: p95_wait_s falls from 188 to 81.4 and max_wait_s from 385 to 245, with unfinished held at 0.0. It does this without loosening the customer promise. Option 3 gives only +0.8 on 3/5 seeds, leaves actual waits unchanged and weakens the promise, so it does not meet the KPI's bar for a change that is worse for customers. The costs of option 1 are real and need a human decision: C's utility falls from 28.8 to 19.0, B's falls slightly, and road violations rise from 25.8 to 34.0. I recommend adopting option 1 together with an explicit human reason for setting aside the B and C votes, or a negotiated mitigation for C, and following up on the rise in road violations.
assumptions: The human operators have the authority to adopt a rule change that some companies voted against, or to negotiate with them.
The 5-seed results represent the demand the town will see next period.
Companies will not change their behaviour (for example, parking strategy) in ways that cancel out the measured gain.
The increase in road violations does not reflect a safety problem serious enough to outweigh the customer gains.

unknowns: Why road violations rise from 25.8 to 34.0 under option 1, and whether any of them are safety-relevant.
Why C loses so much utility under option 1, and whether a mitigation would win B's or C's agreement (for example, a different eviction order or compensation).
Whether the constitution or the companies accept a human override of a rule change that a majority voted against.
Each company's future behaviour policy, including whether they would adapt their parking or routing to block_k 2.
How customers perceive a 150 s pickup promise compared with 120 s, beyond the measured wait times.
Next period's demand level and pattern. Only 5 seeds were measured, so robustness under different loads is unknown.
The combined effect of options 1 and 3, and intermediate settings such as other block_k values, which were not measured.
